submitter: bugs_open/477 lane. Step A (deleting the false promise from the confirm pages) was submitted separately as corr eee96972 and committed 76ec663d3. This is step B: the mechanism that makes the promise true.
rationale:
STEP B OF THREE: build the follow-up email the confirm button claims to suppress, and SEED IT DISABLED.

WHY IT IS A NEW ACTION AND NOT CONFIG. The bug file says a follow-up is "mostly seeding rather than Go" because a mail action already exists. That is wrong, and it is the first thing I checked. SendDeliveryEmailAction calls delivery.Claim, which calls StampHandover, which claims the row `WHERE handed_over_at IS NULL` and returns ErrAlreadyDelivered otherwise (platform/delivery/prepare.go:261-267). Every site a follow-up targets is by definition already handed over, so the existing action refuses, by design, exactly the population the follow-up exists for. I considered and REJECTED making the delivery send skippable by config: that would remove the guard that stops a retry double-emailing a customer, on the estate's only customer-facing mail path, to save one file. Two different claims on two different columns is the honest shape.

WHERE THE BUG ACTUALLY CLOSES. `transfer_confirmed_at IS NULL` is re-checked INSIDE ClaimFollowup's UPDATE, not only in the scheduler's pre_query. That is the whole point: a scheduler selects candidates and then dispatches, and a customer who presses the confirm button in the gap between the two must not be emailed. A pre-query filter cannot promise that; the UPDATE can. This is the first reader sites.transfer_confirmed_at has ever had, and it is in the only race-free position.

THE RISK IS AT-MOST-ONCE, AND IT IS BUILT THE WAY THE ESTATE ALREADY KNOWS WORKS. A scheduled thing that emails customers fails badly not by never sending but by sending nightly. delivery-email-sender is safe because the handover stamp claims the row; a scheduled sender has no equivalent unless one is built. So the claim is `UPDATE sites SET followup_sent_at = $2 WHERE id = $1 AND … AND followup_sent_at IS NULL RETURNING …` — at most one statement can win, a concurrent second caller blocks, re-evaluates after commit and matches nothing. No timestamp takes part in deciding the winner; StampHandover's own comment records what happened when an earlier version tried that (two callers with the same `now` both read themselves as the winner). The two timestamp predicates present (`handed_over_at <= $3` for due-ness, `live_link_expires_at > $2` so the email cannot carry an already-dead confirm link) are membership tests, and the header says so explicitly.

PROVEN AGAINST REAL POSTGRES, NOT ONLY sqlmock, because this package's own opening comment says a mock cannot assert a SQL-level property. Inside a rolled-back transaction: five fixture sites (due / confirmed / already-sent / too-early / window-closed) each claim exactly what they should; the site that won is re-claimed and gets zero, which is the at-most-once property itself; and a NEGATIVE CONTROL drops only the suppression predicate and shows the confirmed site then DOES claim — so the refusals are that predicate's doing and not a fixture that could never have claimed anything. Rollback verified: 60 sites before and after, column gone.

THREE MUTATIONS, EACH CAUGHT. Drop `transfer_confirmed_at IS NULL` from the claim: two tests fail. Drop `followup_sent_at IS NULL`: three fail. Drop ErrFollowupSuppressed from the action's quiet-refusal switch: the refusal test fails. I report this because the sqlmock half of these tests pins SQL text, which is a weak witness on its own, and the mutations plus the Postgres run are what make it more than a spelling check.

DISABLED, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN. The owner has NOT ruled. His words were "maybe repeat them in the first follow up email that would normally go a week or so later" — a suggestion in passing, which is what caused the bug to be filed. So: the scheduled_tasks row ships `enabled = false`, 775's verify ABORTS if it is anything else, and the Go action REFUSES to run without `followup_after_days` rather than defaulting — so the placeholder 7 in the seed cannot quietly become his decision. Enabling is one UPDATE after three stated conditions, and one of them is that he has been told the first run emails him.

⚠ AND I MUST DISCLOSE THAT IT CANNOT CURRENTLY REACH ANYBODY. `[MEASURED 2026-09-04]` build_queue — the ONLY permitted recipient source (651's header, corrected 2026-08-31 under bugs_open/420; sites.email is explicitly forbidden) — has ZERO rows for idea.uk, the only site ever handed over, because it was our own rehearsal site delivered to a hand-typed address and never went through the order pipeline. I found this by running the pre_query with a DEMAND CONTROL (the same query at interval '0 days', which had to return idea.uk and returned nothing); without that control the zero reads as "nothing due" for ever. The obvious fallback also fails, and I measured rather than assumed it: the delivery run does record the address it used, but the oldest row in orchestration_states is under 24 hours old (6,662 rows, oldest 2026-09-03 11:47Z, stale-orchestration-reaper every 180s), so a 7-day-later follow-up looks for it six days after it was reaped. THE REAL GAP is that the estate has no durable record of who a delivered site was delivered to. The structural fix is to stamp the recipient onto the site row in the same statement that stamps handed_over_at — that is platform/delivery/prepare.go, the site_delivery_and_editor lane's surface, and it is ROUTED TO THEM rather than made here. 775's verify reports the gap on every apply (1 of 1 today) so it cannot go quiet. I would rather ship a correct mechanism with a stated empty population than widen the recipient rule myself on a path that emails customers.

CONSUMERS TOLD, and one of them acted. I told the site_delivery_and_editor lane before writing any SQL against shared config, because a third instance of this same false promise turned out to live in THEIR surface — the live delivery-email-sender body_template said "press the button here so we stop reminding you", which the bug file had not measured and which is the only copy of it a human has actually read (the rehearsal email carried it). They shipped it as migration 776, anchored on the verbatim line and aborting if it had moved. Nothing in this submission touches prepare.go, send_delivery_email_action.go or that template. The one place I would have had to touch prepare.go — its unexported tokenURL — I deliberately did not: ConfirmTokenURL is a validating equivalent added to handover.go instead, with a comment saying the two must be collapsed once that lane is out of the file, because a same-file edit from two awake lanes is how one lane's work rides into the other's commit.

SCOPE. I do not believe this needs an RFC and I want that judged rather than assumed. It adds no authority to a shared seam: a new registered action reachable by nothing until a seed names it, one new nullable column, and an agent whose schedule is off. It converges no producers and changes no existing contract's guarantees. The optional-key budget is untouched (the InputSpec declares zero optional keys) and the cron parity tests pass.

plan.summary: Add the follow-up email as its own action with its own once-only claim, suppressed by transfer_confirmed_at inside the claim statement; seed the agent and its schedule DISABLED pending the owner's interval ruling; and report, on every apply, the population it cannot currently reach.

edits.rationale: The at-most-once claim, in the package whose SQL semantics are tested against real Postgres. Claims on `followup_sent_at IS NULL` exactly as StampHandover claims on `handed_over_at IS NULL`; re-checks `transfer_confirmed_at IS NULL` in the same statement (the suppression, race-free); refuses a site past live_link_expires_at IN THE CLAIM so a site that would carry a dead link is never stamped by a run that was never going to send. On zero rows it reads the row and classifies the refusal, because unlike the customer-facing token errors there is no oracle to protect here — the reader is an operator, and a silent scheduler is undiagnosable. A missing site is deliberately NOT one of the four refusals.

A validating builder for the /c/ link. An empty host yields "https:///c/<token>" — well formed, dead, and invisible until a customer clicks it — so it returns an error instead. It DUPLICATES prepare.go's unexported tokenURL, and the comment says so, why (the 475 lane is editing that file this week and a same-file edit from two lanes is how one gets swallowed), and that they must be collapsed. Disclosed rather than hidden: two builders for one customer link is a drift risk whose failure mode is a link that goes somewhere else.

The action. ORDER is inherited from the delivery send and for the same reason: sender constructed FIRST, then the template-vs-links check, THEN the claim — because the claim's stamp deliberately stands even if the send fails (for a chase email, not sending beats sending twice), so anything discoverable beforehand must be discovered beforehand. followup_after_days is REQUIRED with no default: the interval is the owner's undecided question and a compiled-in guess would silently become the answer. The four claim refusals return sent=false with a reason rather than an error, because on a scheduled run refusing is the common case and turning correct behaviour into failed work items makes the queue unreadable. The email carries {{instructions_url}} and never the instructions themselves (bugs_open/475: a copy the customer already holds cannot be corrected).
edits.sketch:
newDeliverySender()            // before the claim
for _, l := range links {…}    // refuse an unfillable placeholder, before the claim
prepared, err := delivery.ClaimFollowup(ctx, db, siteID, now.Add(-days*24h), now)
switch { case errors.Is(err, delivery.ErrFollowupSuppressed), …:
	return map[string]any{"sent": false, "reason": err.Error()}, nil }
confirmToken := delivery.MintToken(…, prepared.LiveLinkExpiresAt, false, "followup-email")
// fresh token: plaintext is never stored, so the original link cannot be reproduced

edits.rationale: Registration, with a comment saying why it is not a config variant of send_delivery_email. The registry is the file every action lane touches, so this is the one same-file passenger risk in the change and it is one entry.
edits.sketch: "send_followup_email": {Handler: SendFollowupEmailAction, Category: "site", Description: "Claim a site's once-only post-delivery follow-up (suppressed by transfer_confirmed_at) and send it…", IsLocal: true},

edits.rationale: The claim column. Nullable, no default, no backfill — every existing row reads 'no follow-up claimed', which is true of all 60. A DEFAULT of now() would mark every site as already followed up and NOT NULL would force a backfill meaning the same, so the verify REFUSES both, plus non-timestamptz, plus any row already stamped. Verify is a DO block, not SELECTs: ON_ERROR_STOP ignores a non-empty result set, so a SELECT-based verify reports and commits anyway. Dry-running this file caught a real defect before it applied — a PL/pgSQL variable named is_nullable is ambiguous against information_schema.columns' own column and Postgres refuses the whole block. ROLLBACK sidecar refuses if any row is stamped or the schedule is enabled.

The agent and its schedule, seeded DISABLED, modelled on zip-link-refresh (the estate's only other site-selecting scheduled sender). Refuses to apply without 774. The verify ABORTS if enabled is anything but false — the load-bearing assertion, because if this ever ships enabled it emails a customer within six hours and nobody decided to. It also refuses a template that promises reminders will stop, since this email IS the reminder. The pre_query is documented as a CANDIDATE FILTER whose predicates are all repeated in the claim, and it takes the recipient from build_queue.direction->>'customer_email', never sites.email. It reports the unreachable population on every apply (1 of 1 today) rather than letting an empty selection read as 'nothing due'. Also fixed before shipping: an earlier draft derived live_site_url from publish_target, which holds a WORKER NAME ('b2worker'), so it would have emailed a customer that word as their website address.

The delivery-package half. Its comment states in situ what sqlmock CANNOT prove here (a mock asserts the SQL sent, not what Postgres does with it) and points at the rolled-back real-Postgres run that does prove it. The refusal-ORDERING case sets BOTH stamps and a closed window on purpose: with only transfer_confirmed_at set it would pass under any switch order, and the test's name ('confirmed wins over everything') would be a claim its own fixture never made. A missing site is asserted NOT to be any of the four refusals, because flattening it into 'not due' would hide a bad site_id in a scheduled run for ever.
edits.sketch:
{"confirmed wins over everything", now, now, now.Add(-60*24h), now.Add(-2*24h), ErrFollowupSuppressed},
// both stamps + a closed window: the only fixture that actually tests the order

edits.rationale: The action half. Order is asserted by what does NOT happen: sqlmock is given NO expectations, so any database touch fails the test — if the order were reversed, the site's one follow-up would be consumed by a run that then found it could not send. Each of the four claim refusals is asserted to send nothing AND not to be an error. Missing/zero/negative/nonsense intervals all refuse before the database is touched. An unfillable placeholder refuses before the claim, and the error is asserted to say 'Nothing was claimed' so an operator knows the site is still reachable. The happy-path regex pins BOTH safety predicates; a comment in situ says a regex over SQL a mock received is a weak witness and names the Postgres run that carries the real proof.
edits.sketch:
mock.ExpectQuery(`(?s)UPDATE sites.*transfer_confirmed_at IS NULL.*followup_sent_at IS NULL`)
if err := mock.ExpectationsWereMet(); err != nil { t.Fatalf("the database was touched before the sender was built: %v", err) }

grounded_in: platform/delivery/prepare.go:261-267 — Claim -> StampHandover -> `if h.AlreadyHandedOver { return Prepared{}, ErrAlreadyDelivered }`. This is why the existing mail action cannot be reused.
platform/delivery/handover.go:159-205 — StampHandover's claim and its comment on why the WHERE clause and not a timestamp comparison decides the winner; ClaimFollowup copies the pattern and cites it.

651_delivery_review_and_email_agents_HOLD.sql:41-47 — 'customer_email SOURCE (corrected 2026-08-31, bugs_open/420): take it from SELECT direction->>customer_email FROM build_queue WHERE domain=$1 — NEVER from sites.email.'

Real Postgres, rolled back, 2026-09-04 — five fixture cases all correct; the winning site re-claimed returns 0; NEGATIVE CONTROL: with only `transfer_confirmed_at IS NULL` removed, the confirmed site DOES claim (so the refusal is that predicate's doing). Rollback verified: sites total 60 before and after, column absent.

Mutation runs, 2026-09-04 — drop the suppression predicate: TestClaimFollowupReturnsTheLiveLinkWindow + TestSendFollowupEmailSendsTheFilledBody FAIL. Drop the at-most-once predicate: three delivery tests FAIL. Drop ErrFollowupSuppressed from the action's quiet switch: TestSendFollowupEmailRefusalsSendNothingAndAreNotErrors FAILS.

build_queue, live, 2026-09-04 — ZERO rows for idea.uk (`SELECT count(*) FROM build_queue WHERE lower(domain)=lower('idea.uk')`), the only site with handed_over_at set. Found by a demand control: the pre_query at interval '0 days' had to return it and returned nothing.

orchestration_states, live, 2026-09-04 — `SELECT min(created_at), count(*)` = 2026-09-03 11:47:55Z, 6,662 rows. Under 24 hours of history, so it cannot be the recipient source for a 7-day-later follow-up.

sites, live, 2026-09-04 — boxingonline.com publish_target='b2worker', publish_project='boxingonline.ugg2.com'; idea.uk has BOTH empty. This is what made the first draft's live_site_url derivation wrong, and it is why the shipped one is 'https://' || domain, matching the operator recipe the delivery email itself used (RUNBOOK_site_delivery_and_editor.md:425).

cmd/config-key-audit parity tests, 2026-09-04 — TestBudgetCronCountsLiteralMatchesTheRegistry, TestBudgetCronAgreesWithTheGoDetector, TestCronCheckDeclaredListMatchesTheRegistry all PASS with the new action registered (its InputSpec declares zero optional keys, so the RFC_022 budget is untouched).
